paras: The manhunt for Charles Gilmor took place around Martinsville in June 1881, when posses of citizens hunted Gilmor, a Black man, after he was accused of trying to rape Miss Winchester in her father's house. No capture or violence against him was reported, but the Chicago Daily Tribune printed the news under a headline saying such men should be hanged when caught.

The news came in a dispatch from Greensboro, North Carolina, dated June 24, which did not name the state or county of Martinsville. The dispatch opened with the recent lynching of two men in Stokes County for rape and another lynching two weeks earlier, and with a rape accusation against a Black man named William Gauch near Hillsboro.

According to the dispatch, on the evening of June 23 Gilmor entered the house of Prince Winchester while Winchester and his wife were away and their daughter was alone. Miss Winchester, who knew him, was said to have ordered him out, after which he threatened her and attempted to assault her while she screamed for help. The dispatch said he leapt from a rear window as neighbors drawn by her screams entered the house.
"Posses of citizens have been hunting him all day," the dispatch reported.
No report of Gilmor's capture, arrest, trial or death appears in the coverage.

The only report found ran in the Chicago Daily Tribune on June 27, 1881, under the headline "Wretches Who Should Be Hung When Caught." The dispatch treated the accusation as established fact, spoke of Gilmor's "devilish design," and asserted without attribution that he had twice been convicted of attempted rape and rape. By framing the case as proof that recent lynchings had not had "the effect looked for by the lynchers," the dispatch placed the manhunt within an argument for lynching.
